speechtext: We get into a far better position, and therefore there is all the more reason for accepting it, and it would be all the more disgraceful if we retired from it. Because it is better for us is surely not a reason why we should retire from it. Would the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) have us say to the Grand Trunk: We made you an offer in the month of July, 1918; we let it stand open until now; now you come forward and accept it and give us a little better terms. If you had accepted it before, we would have taken it, but as you did not accept it before, and now that you give us a little better terms, we will not accept it.	[DOT]
That is neither law nor business. The moment the Grand Trunk people refused the offer of July 11, 1918, that was the end of the transaction, and we were not bound by it any longer.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not contend that
we were bound.

Then, why is the
minister saying that we should take it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Because we left the offer open. We could have retreated or withdrawn from it at any minute.
It was closed. We made an offer; it was not accepted; that is the end of it; it is not open any longer.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is not open unless
we leave it open.

It is not open.
We made them an offer; that is all we could do about the matter. The company refused it; that is the end of it in law.	i

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is, unless they know that we are keeping it open, and they knew it by the negotiations. The hon. gentleman knew that, and I will tell him why. In the speech of the Minister of Finance of that day, he made it clear that the position of the Government at that time was

represented in the letter of July 11, and ithat was months .afterwards. Therefore, the hon. gentleman knew that the offer was open.
I have stated my position ar.d my position is right; that is the .end of it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is more Scotch finality than Scotch logic in the hon. member

Now that that point is settled, will the minister allow me to revert to my question of a moment ago, in answer to which he said: We are not going to transfer any of the stock that the Government is going to acquire. Did I understand him to say that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is right.

Then what is meant by clause 5 of the resolution:
That the value, if any, of the first, second and third preference stocks and the common or ordinary stock of the Grand Trunk now issued and outstanding to the face values above mentioned (hereafter together called the "preference and common stock"), shall be determined by a board of three arbitrators, one to be appointed by the Government, one by the Grand Trunk, and the third by the two so appointed, or, failing agreement, by judges to be designated in the said agreement. No guaranteed stock, to an amount not exceeding the value, if any, so determined, carrying a dividend as hereinbefore authorized shall be distributed among the holders of the preference and common stock, upon the transfer to or vesting in the Government of such stock, in proportions which shall be determined by the arbitrators.
Then by a subsequent clause the Government may call in at par, after thirty years and1 upon six months' notice, any of the stock it desires. 'The purpose of the Government in taking over this stock is simply to turn it into a new form of stock to be called the new guaranteed stock, which the Government intends to guarantee and1 then transfer it to the holders of the common, first, second and1 third preference stocks.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no objection at all to the hon. gentleman asking me a question but he should not make so long a speech as to half empty the House before I get through with inline.
Thank you, I will come back.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What 'the hon. member asked me first was whether we were going to' transfer to somebody else the stock that we acquired.

No. The minister said a moment ago that the Government was not

going to transfer any of the stock that they acquired.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is absolutely true. We acquire the voting stock, the controlling stock that makes us the owners of the whole Grand Trunk system. We keep that right here in the possession of the people of Canada. The holders of that stock, if they are awarded anything 'by the 'arbitration receive from us new non-voting certificates, or non-voting stock. But, surely, issuing a new stock is not transferring the old stock. The new stock is a different one altogether. We only issue a 4 per cent stock, which *to-day would sell in the neighbourhood of 70, and we issue it only for the value of the stock we acquire. The difference is clear profit to the people of Canada. I hope the hon. member understands that. He surely sees that the issue of the new non-voting stock to men who were the holders of the controlling interest-hearing stock is not transferring the old controlling interest-bearing stock-far from, it.
How is it proposed to get the holders of the guaranteed stock to release their voting power?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They must do that before the transaction is binding upon the Covernment. The guaranted stockholders must themselves surrender that power, and until they do so the guarantee of the Government does not go into effect.
There is a great number of them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and it is a difficult matter. The voting power is an element of value highly prized, I am advised, by the holders of that stock, and the same is true* of all the stocks in connection with the road. In lieu of surrendering this voting power they get the guarantee of the Government only for their 4 per cent dividend.

What would be the
situation if some of them refused to surrender t'heir voting power?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Until that is done the agreement would not take effect. As I apprehend the legal position, it must all be surrendered before the agreement can take effect. We could not agree that we would go ahead and guarantee in respect of those who surrender their voting power and leave others in partial control of the road.
One man might hold up the whole deal?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He might, I -could- not say: but I do not think it is probable.
Is provision made for any delay?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not yet, but that will be a ' subject to be taken care of in the agreement itself. Hon. gentlemen will see from the very pertinent query of my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) that it is important that some special inducement be given to the holders of the stock who have this special element of value in it, the voting power, in order that the transaction will not be impeded or wholly destroyed by the obstinacy of some shareholders. Any voting power that is now resident in the holders of the debenture stock must also be given up. They in turn get perhaps a slight accretion to their stock, because it also is guaranteed. So the transaction is fair in every respect. Those men who inevitably get a little accretion of value to their stock have to give up in lieu thereof all the control they heretofore exercised in connection with the enterprise. That control is much more highly valued in the Mother Country than it is in Canada.
Now I come to another phase of the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding). He is afraid, he says, of arbitration. Well, what plan does he suggest to get at the value when we cannot agree upon it? He is afraid of arbitration. Arbitration is not only the method employed in the past in similar transactions, one of which he referred to, but it is the method embedded in the legislation of this country everywhere in the case of acquirement of land or property. It is universally and historically recognized as the best, fairest, and the only way for determining disputed claims. Why is he afraid of an arbitration in connection with the Grand Trunk? What is the special reason attending the acquisition of the Grand Trunk railway that makes arbitration unsuited for the solution of the problem?
Mr. JACOBS- Why not liquidation instead?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Liquidation? Well, the leader of the Opposition told us yesterday that it was a shameful and disgraceful thing to let the Grand Trunk Pacific go info a receivership. If that was disgraceful, what would he say of letting the Grand Trunk go into a receivership?
I said the methods by which it was done were disgraceful, not the letting it go into a receivership. If my hon. friend will read my statement he will see I said I was not afraid of a receivership.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have repeated exactly what he said, that letting the Grand Trunk go into a receivership was disgraceful.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) says, why not let the Grand Trunk go into a receivership? Well, if hon. gentlemen will take that stand, and we know exactly where they are at, it is worth discussing. Why not let the Grand Trunk go into a receivership? Does the hon. gentleman know what would almost inevitably result if it did?

It would save us many
millions of dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It would for us at the moment, and perhaps make many millions for the Canadian Pacific Railway. That would be one very probable result.
Mr. JACOBS': We would acquire the company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Why would not the Canadian Pacific acquire it?
We could acquire it better.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We can pay more for it than they?
We are the Government of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We would acquire it by main force?
No, by law.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is main force. Before discussing that further I said a moment ago that I quoted the leader of the Opposition correctly, when he said that, letting the Grand Trunk Pacific go into a receivership was disgraceful. Here is what he said:
Mr. Rowell:	That is what your argument
leads to.
Mr. McKenzie:	Not at all. The President
of the Council as a member of the Government put it in the hands of the receiver and we say that was a disgraceful and unbusinesslike thing to do. But once it is in the hands of the receiver it must be dealt with in a businesslike way.
There is nothing about method there. The hon. gentleman said that putting it in the hands of the receiver was a disgraceful and unbusinesslike thing to do.

If the hon. gentleman will read further he will see that I said the Government bad not the machinery to deal with such a matter and that it should have gone into the courts where there was
[Mr McKenzie.]
proper provision for it. The whole drift of my statement w-as that the Government should not appoint the receiver.*

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Government was the principal creditor and consequently it was the proper thing that a member of the Government should be apointed receiver,
Mr, McKENZIE:	The receiver was
appointed under the War Measures Act. At least, we were told so a thousand times by the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly, but it went through the courts, and the whole transaction and administration of the Grand Trunk Pacific is done through the Exchequer Court just the same as any other receivership.

The	receiver was
appointed hy the Government themselves, which is absolutely without precedent in the history of any country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman suggest that the Government of, Canada, -which was not only the majority creditor but by far the greatest creditor of the Grand Trunk Pacific, should have sat by and let some one else be appointed receiver, responsible for the operation and management of the Grand Trunk Pacific? What kind of Premier would he make who would allow that to be done?

Does the hon. minister think that he can play on conditions of that kind? Supposing there are two creditors of any concern in Canada-and we have an Insolvent Act to-day-one of them with a claim of 510,000 and the other $100. Does my hon. friend mean to say that the creditor with, the claim o,f $10,000 can appoint himself receiver?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, but I say the courts would appoint him receiver 'ahead of the other whose claim was $100.
The court would appoint him receiver, certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In this case, the right receiver is the Government of Canada, is it not?
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Again I compliment the obstinacy of the leader of the Opposition. Now, I was going on to the 'Statement of the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs). His idea is that we should have let the Grand Trunk proceed into liquidation.

I was merely asking the simple question why it was not done in that

way. I shall express my own views later without the assistance of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman will answer my question. I shall answer him first: I am not in favour of that proposition. Is he in favour of it or not?
I will express my opinion in regard to that later on. I am trying to marshall my arguments.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So that the House has very little information a.s to where the hon. gentleman stands on the question of a receivership for the Grand Trunk.
And I do not think that the House has any information as to the minister's position either.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I stated my position; I said I am opposed to it. What more does he want?
Because the minister is Afraid of the Canadian Pacific Railway acquiring the road?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is one powerful reason.
That was not the reason that actuated my hon. friend when he took over the Canadian Northern.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It was one powerful [DOT]reason there as well. Is that- frank enough?
I beg your pardon, I meant *to say the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no danger of the Canadian Pacific Railway acquiring the Grand Trunk Pacific alone. The hon. gentleman knows more about the business [DOT]acumen of the Canadian Pacific Railway *Company than to think that they would *acquire a limping, halting, utterly bankrupt institution like the Grand Trunk Pacific and leave the Grand Trunk free of obligations.

Inasmuch as the minister, [DOT]as I understand, used to act as solicitor *for the Canadian Pacific railway he would *know more about their methods than I do.
' Mr. MEIGHEN: On no occasion in the [DOT]world have I ever acted' as solicitor for *the Canadian Pacific railway. I am afraid there are very few more holes for the hon. gentlemen to fall into. Now my hon. friend evidently has in the back of his head exactly the practical business objections to a receivership of the Grand Trunk railway. The same objections obtained in the case of the Canadian Northern, but
they obtain with greater force in the case of the Grand Trunk. The policy of standing by and letting the wreck proceed was a policy of drifting the whole institution into the mouth of the Canadian Pacific Railway.	_
Now, it is said that this is too favourable for the Grand Trunk's shareholders. Well, it will appeal to any one of ordinary forethought and independent opinion that if *this was a very favourable proposition for the Grand Trunk Company they would not have waited1 sixteen months to accept it. I should1 like hon. members to read the *comments of the president of the Grand Trunk-comments dictated by and undoubtedly in accordance with the sentiments of the Grand Trunk directors' and shareholders-on the offer made by the Government on the 11th July. Did they think it was a favourable offer? Throughout Great Britain the cry of confiscation was raised, and at a meeting of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk-indeed at [DOT]more than one,-.the epithets hurled at the Government of Canada for their parsimony, unfairness and lack of generosity to the [DOT]shareholders of the Grand Trunk were far from complimentary to this country. They were, in my opinion, wholly unjustified. But whatever may be the ideas of hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to the generosity of the offer, now that it is accepted, they are very, very antithetical to the opinions of the Grand Trunk Company,-president, directors and shareholders alike. The *company waited eighteen months before giving even an intimation that there was a probability of acceptance. One condition after the other was tried, and does any one suggest for a moment that indications were that the transaction was closed ? I recall myself an editorial in the Toronto Globe- and in newspaper after newspaper throughout the country the same thing was urged calling upon the Government to stand firm by its offer. The Government were called upon not to move. They were told: "All you have to do is to stand firm; your offer is fair; stand right to it and the Grand Trunk will have to come to terms." Did that indicate that everything was closed ? Never for one day was there any intimation given or impression left that negotiations with the Grand Trunk were closed or that any offer made by the Government was modified or withdrawn.. The country knew, and has known since July, 1918,-yes, and before-that negotiations were proceeding and that the Grand Trunk turned them over time and again, and that there was no modi-

fication in the position of the Government. The hope was universally expressed that there would be no modification, and the hope of the people of Canada is realized to-day; and
Can the minister tell me if the Grand Trunk was ever in negotiation with the Canadian Pacific Railway looking to the acquisition by that company of the Grand Trunk?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know of no negotiations. It would not likely be through the instrumentality of a member of the Government, nor would such negotiations be even known to a member of the Government. That is not the way in which great companies negotiate. They do not negotiate through the medium of a competitor.
I am asking my hon. friend if he has any personal knowledge.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no personal knowledge. It would be wholly improbable, indeed, wholly inconceivable that I should have.

As a purchaser the minister,
I should think, would have obtained some information as to whether this company was being offered to another concern.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Canadian Pacific Railway never vouchsafed me any information on the subject. I do not know whether they favoured my hon. friend with information.
Mr. Smithers did not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Now, the hon. member for Queen's and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding) is very distrustful of arbitration, and in the course of his remarks to-day he made some reference to the procedure of the Government in referring the Canadian Northern outstanding shares to arbitration some two years ago. He told us that the Drayton-Acworth report found these shares tfT be valueless and he said: that we should not have paid anything for them.
The Drayton-Aeworth report recommended the Government to submit the value of these shares to arbitration. The Government pursued the recommendation of the Drayton-Aeworth report. In any event would the hon. member suggest to this House that the Government would be justified in taking the report of officers appointed and paid by themselves upon evidence respecting which the Canadian Northern had no right and no duty to appear and show the value of the shares; in other words-, to take an ex parte report, as far as the shareholders 
were concerned, and, acting upon that report, to declare that there was no value in these shares? To do so would' be to put the Government of Canada in a position that they never could defend to the shareholders, to the country, ~or to the world at large. When a man's property is taken a fundamental principle ot British justice is that he shall have a tribunal before which he may go and prove the value of his property if he -can. There was no such tribunal until the board of arbitration was appointed. The Drayton-Aeworth -commission was no such tribunal. The shareholders cut no figure and had no place before that commission. It was not within the purview of the commission to hear the shareholders as to the value of their shares and they did not hear them. Consequently it would have been a flagrant and gros-s injustice on the part of the Government to have declared no value and to have expropriated by brute force the property of their citizens. Instead of doing that they appointed a board of arbitration and a board of high standing. My hon. friend does not for a moment impugn the high standing and probity of any member of that commission through whose examination and determination the amount to be paid was arrived at.
The same thing will be done in this case. The same procedure is proposed in this resolution. It is honourable procedure; it is British procedure; it is fairness; it is justice and it is no more.
If these resolutions and the Bill are passed this country will have a real system; it will have a rounded system; it will have a complete system; it will have a system one-half giving its tribute to the other half, ane gathering traffic in one part of Canada which will be transported over the road of the other and the other gathering traffic in the other part of Canada for interchange.
It will save this- country in capital investment $100,000,000 in five years. The interest on this that will be saved, at even the present rates, will be far more than sufficient to take care of the obligations in all probability that we will be under as a result of the award of the board of arbitration. With respect to the money that will be saved to Canada by amalgamation, the money that otherwise we must invest in additions to the present Canadian railway system, the money that will be invested in duplication and. consequently wasted, the money that will be saved by reason of the acquisition of the Grand Trunk railway, this country

will save in annual interest more than will be sufficient to pay the award of the arbitration and the interest on the guaranteed stock and1 besides in all human probability, it will possibly save the country some millions more. Is that not a good transaction? Is that not fair business? Is it not right and proper that economies and amalgamations should be made? Is it not right and proper that duplicate capital investment should be avoided? Is it not right and proper that an inchoate system should be made complete? Is not arbitration the proper way? That is in a nutshell the proposal of this resolution and with the utmost confidence I commend it to the consideration of the House at this session of Parliament. This is just as valid, just as good a session as any other; it is a session in which every hon. member who draws his indemnity from the country should feel it his duty to give a reasonable proportion of his time to the public business. At this session it is only right and just that hon. members should give their attention to this question and devote to it all necessary time to enable them to come to a just conclusion.

I commend 'the lecture of my hon. friend respecting absentees to the men who should occupy the seats behind him. There are one or two points in the observations of my hon. friend to which I should make a passing allusion. First in regard to arbitration. The point I made concerning arbitration was that when a stock, known to be not worth any money, was capable of being adjudged for the reasons presented by an honourable board of arbitration as worth $10,000,000 or $11,000,000 we had some reason for anxiety as to what might be the outcome of an arbitration in respect to these voluminous stocks of the Grand Trunk Railway Company which had some money value at some time. Therefore I suggested that the House ought not to be left in doubt as to the extent of the obligations and the risk we are assuming under those obligations and that the award of the arbitrators should be subject to the approval of the House of Commons of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman suggest that it .should be subject to the approval of the shareholders?
They are not bound to accept it if they do not want to.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
But they are.
69	I
I would not force it on the shareholders. I would not force the shareholders to take any value for it that they did not want to take.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then what is the good of arbitration?
Well, my hon. friend can answer; he is proposing arbitration. What is the good of the whole proceeding in view of the understanding which has been arrived at?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: An arbitration held under such conditions that the result is binding on nobody has no sense at all, but an arbitration on the principle that the result binds both is an arbitration that is final and has some object in view.
My answer is that the people of Canada, through their representatives, will say that Parliament should be called upon to vote for any necessary sum of money with a full knowledge of what that sum is.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And the shareholders should not be given the right to say whether they would accept it or not?
I have no objection to the shareholders standing out for a different report.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then you will have no arbitration.

With reference to the 4 per cent guaranteed stock, if my hon. friend wants to buy anything and he finds what the market value is he will be doing no injustice to anybody if he gets it at that value. The market value of that stock in London was 45. There would toe no injustice to anybody if you had arranged with a broker and he had bought that stock at 45, 46 or 47.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That was considered and found to be absolutely impossible.
There was nothing impossible about it at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The dealing in the stock of the Grand Trunk during the last five years has been almost infinitesimal. I have that from the officers of the Grand Trunk themselves. Because of the market conditions in Great Britain to-day it is impracticable. The proportion of these stocks that has been dealt in during the last five years is negligible. The ratio to the whole amount of the stock is very small and these stocks are owned not by thousands but hundreds of thousands of people.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We do not.

We are going to convert the stock into a stock guaranteed by the Government of Canada and paying four per cent. In normal times a four per cent government guaranteed stock is worth par. I do not think it would 'be worth that at this moment. Even with the guarantee of the Government of Canada I have estimated it at something less than 85 or even 90. I assumed it might go to 90 not long after this thing is consummated, but suppose we take it at 85, the difference between the 40 quoted a few days ago and the 90 or 85, say, that the stock should be worth at no distant date will be 40 points.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend
permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Without the impression produced by the Government's guarantee at all that stock stood at 1061 not long ago.
How long ago?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It was at 1011 in 1904 and in 1902 it was at 106|.
What has that- to do with the question?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In 1906 the first preference stock stood at 123. It is a matter of the rate of interest.

It is a matter of market value. Here is stock which the Government desire to secure quoted on the money market at 45, later on at 48, and hon. gentlemen opposite, by this legislation, are causing it now to Teach a value of 85 or 90. Does my hon, friend say that the guaranteed four per cent bonds of Canada are not worth 85? Will he say that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think the stock has sold. for that at all.
The hon. gentleman thinks it may reach 85?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Without the guarantee at all it was worth that much. Then if money comes down in value-
If it was worth that much before the guarantee it will be worth more after the guarantee.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It depends on the rate of interest.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is an easy matter
when you have a small road to merge it because you do not in any way detract from the earning power of that road, but where you have -a great system, and where it prob-

ably will be necessary to dismantle lines, you do detract from the earning power-

It is a matter of common notoriety in our railway circles that you have to take certain sections of the road and keep separate accounts as to their earnings. For example, the Minister of Railways has entered into an agreement with a railway company down in New Brunswick which is going to be practically merged with the government system and going to be operated by the Government, and he has got to account separate and apart for the earnings of that company. If my hon. friend says it is utterly impossible, that the thing cannot be done, I must express my amazement, that one who has had such a long experience in railway matters as the hon. gentleman has, should make such a statement.
There is only one point more. My hon. friend finds it exceedingly difficult to discuss any question without introducing a little party politics. I have not made any allusion to party politics, and I have not sought to make any party capital. My hon. friend could not talk about this matter without bringing in the story of the original transaction with the Grand Trunk Pacific -" an utterly unsound and rotten proposition." He did not use the word " rotten," I forget what his term was; at all events, he denounced it. I am not going to spend any time at this hour, six o'clock, in defending that transaction, but the hon. gentleman can read the speech of his colleague, the President of the Privy Council, who yes-day declared it was one of the greatest triumphs in the life of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and for which he would be remembered.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.
After Recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Would the minister in charge inform the committee what, exclusive of the arbitration award, will be the total_ obligations to be assumed by the Dominion when the transaction is completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: I mean the total bond obligations against the undertaking?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We do not assume any bonds at all; they are a charge against the road.
That is what I mean, the bonds against the road.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: But those bonds continue in perpetuity, so the only liability we assume is the interest on them.
But the interest falls due.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes. We assume that, but we do not assume the principal. For instance, the bonds on the Grand Trunk Pacific fall due in a certain number of years, but these other bonds of which we. have been speaking are in perpetuity.

But, Mr. Chairman, there' is a statement in this book giving the total amount of liabilities, and it is useless for the minister to quibble in that way. Can he tell me the amount of obligations the country will assume, without taking into account the amount the arbitrators may award?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The only amounts that we assume or are liable for are interest-
Interest on how much?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: Will the country also assume this item of unsecured notes payable amounting to $35,000,000, and equipment trust notes amounting to $6,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The equipment bonds are against the equipment-cars, engines, etc. We do not assume them; they are liable themselves.

Who is "liable themselves"? Tlhe equipment is not going to pay out any money. The company will naturally have to pay interest on the equipment and pay off the (bonds. The equipment is not the company itself.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

I think the minister is getting ready to answer me, Mr. Chairman.
I notice that $504,000,000 in one place and $707,000,000 in another place are given as the liabilities that are being assumed. I want to know whether the Government understands that that is the total obligation to be assumed by the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I must repeat that the only liability the country assumes is to pay in perpetuity the interest of $7,000,000 on the debenture stock and of $2,500,000 on the other stock. The other liabilities take care of themselves. For instance, the mortgage on the equipment; we are not assuming any liability in regard to that other than is covered by the equipment bonds. The interest, of course, becomes due on that mortgage, but we are not making the Government liable for the principal.

I think the minister will agree with me that the new company or the old company is liable for all the amounts set out here as chargeable to the company. In that connection there is an item of something like $210,000,000 in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific. If we deduct from that the amount owing to the Dominion we arrive at one basis of ascertaining how much greater obligations the country is assuming in taking over this undertaking. We know that we are not getting it for nothing; we are assuming obligations. What is the sum total of the obligations as figured by the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
That information is given on page 37 of this sessional paper. It shows the assets and liabilities, but we are only assuming the interest on those liabilities. While it shows a total of $124,000,000 of guaranteed stock and 4 per cent first, second and third preference stock, that is to be the subject of arbitration. Whatever amount the arbitrators decide, if any, as the interest on that stock, we of course will assume. The funded debt I have just mentioned to the hon. member, we assume a liability of $7,000,000 on that. While it shows $155,000,000 as the total amount of that funded debt, yet we do not 
agree to pay that amount in any number of years hereafter, we only agree to pay the interest on it in perpetuity. Then, of course, we do the same in regard to the guaranteed stock. As to the equipment notes and these other items, they are loans against the equipment.
We shall have to pay interest on the equipment bonds, but that is not any permanent liability. I do not know how to explain to the hon. member in any more detail than is shown on this statement which was made out by auditors and which to me is as plain as it can- be made and easily understood.

As clear as mud. If it
is so plain to the minister, how does he get $74000,000 interest on $155,000,000 worth of bonds? The President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) speaks about $200,000,000 being spent in the first, second and third preference common stocks, and in these letters from the company we find they have spent less than $100,000,000. I am endeavouring to bring these wild statements down to something concrete. I should like from the Government a statement as to what they estimate from their own figures as the amount of the total liability on which interest will have to be paid, call it in perpetuity or what you will.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
wants to know what the principal is on which interest will have to be paid. If he will turn to page 38 he will find that the total stock, preference, common and guaranteed, amounts to $241,257,658.27, of which $60,833,332.51 is guaranteed stock. On the latter we shall have to pay in perpetuity interest at the rate of 4 per cent, and the arbitrators will decide as to the value of the balance of the $241,257,658.27. That is, they will decide the value of the first, second and third preference and the common stock, and on whatever valuation they place on those stocks the Government will pay 4 per cent interest. That disposes, so far as I can explain the matter, of the $241,257,658.27. Then we come to the funded debt $155,373,806.20. That is the original debenture issue for the construction of the Grand Trunk and the purchase of the Great Western and the Northern railway forty or fifty years ago. We shall pay on that interest which in round figures amounts to $7,000,000 per annum. Those two amounts represent the capital on which we shall have to paj7 interest, we shall not have to pay interest on any other capital in connection with the Grand Trunk railway. In addition to that there is a large amount of money in equipment, and bonds have been

issued against equipment. That is a part of the operation of the road and interest will have to be paid on the equipment bonds, together with the principal that falls due from year to year. That is explained in the statement, and I do not know that I could give it in any more detail nor explain it any better than it is explained here.
That is not included in the arbitration?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, it is included. The arbitrators will have to take into consideration the physical condition of the road, equipment of all kinds, in fact, everything owned and controlled by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. The equipment is worth so much money less the amount that is against it. That is the way in which the equipment must be taken into consideration, just the same as any other liquid assets the company might have.

The minister is
endeavouring to be clear, but he is not very clear to the committee. To begin with, we all understand that the country pays interest on the guaranteed stock. It also pays interest, whatever happens, on the debenture stock of which there are four kinds. We stop there. The rest, my hon. friend says, is to be settled by arbitration. Supposing the arbitration is held, and the arbitrators, let hs say for the sake of argument, give the company $1,000,000 for the balance, and we pay that $1,000,000. Do we then become owners of the road without any mortgages or any claims of any kind, either on the road or on the common stock, excepting the interest to which I have referred in regard to the guaranteed stock and the debenture stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: To me, the matter is plain, and I think it has been explained many times in this House.
My question can be answered toy "yes" or "no."

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I do not know that you can answer it exactly toy "yes" or "no." The hon. member has, I understand, asked this question: Supposing the arbitrators decide to give an award of $1,000,000 over and above the $7,000,000 and the $2,500,000, what happens then? What happens is this? The first, second and third preference and the common stocks must all be handed over to the Dominion Government; they are our property. In return we issue non-voting stock to the amount that will give $1,000,000 per annum rental. We shall then have all
of those stocks, and we shall be the owners of the road, being the sole shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company.

But have we a clear title?
Mr.-J. D. REID: Certainly we have a clear title, to this extent, that we are the owners of the stock subject to the payment of the interest in perpetuity.
What about the equipment?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Grand Trunk Railway Company owns the equipment, and we are the owners of the Grand Trunk Railway Company; therefore, we own the equipment.
But the equipment is mortgaged.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Of course, we take the equipment subject to whatever may be against it.

Then we shall have very heavy liabilities in addition to the $1,000,900 that we shall have to meet when we begin to operate the road. The minister has the blue-book on his desk. Last night, I endeavoured to get some explanation about the contents of page 51, and I failed to get it. I should like to know from the Minister of Railways whether the stocks of the various subsidiary companies mentioned on page 51 will be transferred to the Government on the settlement by the arbitrators.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The stocks of those subsidiary companies are now owned by the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
On lease?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Some may be lease-owned, but as regards whatever interest in those companies rests at present in the Grand Trunk Railway Company, when we take the stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, we shall stand in the same position as that company does now. Therefore, we become owners in that way.

In some of these companies, the Grand Trunk Railway Company has guaranteed the principal and the interest on certain bonds. Will the Grand Trunk Railway Company, after the Government gets possession of it, be liable for the guarantees that have been given toy that company on those bonds?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The Grand Trunk Railway Company are liable to-day; they will be liable in the future just the same.

When we become the stockholders of the Grand Trunk we shall become liable.
How much will that liability amount to?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The hon. member will find the figures for each road on page 34 of the memoranda. I do not think the total is given.
It is not, and I should like to have that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I will get that.

I have a clipping before me containing some figures which I should like the minister to confirm. The clipping reads:
In the proposed deal .the Government pledges itself to pay 4 per cent on all Grand Trunk debentures, 4 per cent on all guaranteed stock and 4 per cent on the arbitrated value of all other Grand Trunk securities.
Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Interest on the debenture stock and 4 per cent on the guaranteed stock.

It goes- on:
The first item means an annual interest charge of about $6,000,000 ; the second a charge of approximately $2,260,000. The third is a variable quantity. The nominal value of the unguaranteed Grand Trunk securities is about $170,000,000. Figuring on the basis of average stock market quotations for the securities, this value is reduced to less than one-quarter, requiring about $1,350,000 in interest charges. That makes a total of annual obligations in addition to running the road, of about $9,600,-
000.	Subtract the net earnings of the Grand Trunk under company ownership and you have an annual loss of $6,600,000.
If the Government fails to operate the road as economically as the company, this loss will grow. But even on the basis of the Government's own figures and hopes, the Canadian tax-payers are buying, not a profit, but another white elephant for the hungry herd fattening on their diminishing treasury.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Who wrote that out for you?

It has been handed to me. I fancy it was in the Montreal Star, which is usually a pretty good Government supporter, but they balk at this. There are limits beyond which a newspaper supporting the Government cannot go.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I should like the hon. member to ridicule that as it ought to be ridiculed. The idea of a man making a guess at what the arbitrators will award, without anything to go on, and taking that figure to be absolutely found and established, and then proceeding to argue what the deficit will be! More simpering non-

sense can scarcely be conceived, although I have read some in the press that compares with it almost identically. What is the value of reading that out to the Committee? There is nobody here so unintelligent and dense as to be influenced for a second by rubbish of that sort.
From what I can gather, the minister is not in agreement with the article I have read.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I should think not.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Nor anybody else.
Mr.-CAHILL: From my reading of these figures, I come to the conclusion that we are undertaking to pay interest on a total capitalization of $470,000,000 in connection with this transaction. Am I nearly correct?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, the hon. gentleman is wrong.
What is the correct figure?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has been told it at least seven times, and three or four times this evening since eight o'clock.

'I am asking the question again because I did not get it answered. You do not mean to say that you are going to pay interest on the $707,000,000. You say yourself you are going to arbitrate, and if you arbitrate you are taking.into account ' the whole $707,000,000. I am trying to make a deduction to arrive at what will not be arbitrated upon.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The resolution that has been before the hon. gentleman for two days, indeed, since last Friday, sets out definitely in figures that a child could read the exact debenture stock and the rate of interest on it which we undertake to pay, also the exact guaranteed stock with the rate of interest. That is all there is to it. There is no deduction necessary. It is all there in black and white.
Where is it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is in the resolution, and in the letter read in the House last Friday.
I do not' see any mention of it in the resolution at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
On the top of page 10 of to-day's Orders of the Day my hon. friend will find the debenture stocks, and on page 9 the present capital stocks. The letter that was read in the House last Friday says that we pay four per cent on the guaranteed

stock, and interest on the various debenture stocks set out at the top of page 10. There are no deductions to be made. Why ask this question fifty times over?

For the simple reason that there is no person in the Government with sufficient intelligence to answer the question as it should be answered. If the minister, who apparently does not wish to commit the Government as to the extent to which they are being obligated in this transaction, would look at page 39 of 'his own memoranda he will find that there are notes secured and unsecured amounting to $35,000,000. That is not mentioned in the resolution at all. Then there are the Grand Trunk Pacific bonds mentioned in the resolution, so if the minister has read the resolution and the list of other obligations he must know what should be deducted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman says "obligations," I hope he means obligations. The obligations I have already told him, and if I stood here six months I could not tell him any more plainly. It was just as plain as if I had told him that two and three are five. There are other debts of the company, and we take the assets subject to those debts. They are all set out on that page. We do not assume those obligations. The 4 per cent interest on the guaranteed stock becomes our obligation. We take the stock of the Grand Trunk. The company's properties are subject to certain obligations, which are all set out there.
What do they amount to?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The figures are there. Cannot the hon. gentleman read? Do I have to read them over to him?
Cannot you total them up?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is all made up here, but if the hon. gentleman says he cannot read I will read it for him. It is in English, not in Italian or Greek.
Nor in code.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
might be more familiar with it if it was in code. These are the figures.

Northern 4% debenture stock. ..	1,499,979.65
Total debenture stock	$155,373,806.20
That is the debenture stock upon which we oblige ourselves to pay the interest, Let us proceed. On the same page we find 4 per cent guaranteed stock $60,833,332.51. That is the guaranteed stock on which we
pay interest. That is all we oblige ourselves to do. Then there are other debts which the company holds its property subject to, and when we are stockholders the company will hold its property subject to them the same as now. The hon. gentleman wants to know what these debts are. Well, I shall read them to him; they are in English :
Second mtge. equipment bonds

Then there are other liabilities of the company. They follow in order and I may read them if the hon. gentleman thinks it *sounds better for me to read them than for him to read them himself. There are current liabilities, reserves and advances to *controlled 'Companies. I do not think reserves and advances to controlled companies could he described as liabilities, but the current liabilities are:
Interest on capital account accrued	$ 3,123,755.42
Sundry outstanding accounts 15,409,985.97 Wages unpaid at Dec. 1918. ..	3,132,851.84
Overdraft at bank	 1,134,881.12
Against those, all the assets on the other side of the balance sheet are the property of the company. What, then, is the difficulty?
Mr. 'CAHILL: Does the minister say that we are assuming a capital of $500,000,000 on which we must pay interest?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No; not at all.
Then what is the amount? Surely that can be answered. I also want to know what amount is being assumed on account of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know what I can do. I am afraid I must give it up.
Surely some member of the Government can answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have answered it.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cahill) is somewhat confused. He seems to view the matter as an outright purchase. If I understand the subject, we are assuming a liability of interest on a certain amount of securities which to all intents and purposes will be a rental. But there are these last-named securities mentioned by the minister. I understand that

that will stand as a claim against the stock that is still held by the Grand Trunk Pacific. That is what I understand.
Ask the minister if that is what he understands.
He will not answer.
The hon. member (Mr. J. R. Wilson) states his view of the situation. Perhaps the minister will enlighten him.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The whole matter is very plain, and it has been explained so many times that I do not think there is anything that I can add. The Minister of the Interior explained the situation with regard to the Grand Trunk Railway. The Grand Trunk Pacific is a subsidiary of the Grand Trunk, and when we take over the system we shall assume the liabilities in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific. When we take over the Grand Trunk railway we shall assume the interest on all the bonds.
Amounting to how much?

I would have to look it up, but it is probably $6,000,000 or $7,000,000 per annum. Until the war the Grand Trunk Pacific was able to meet operating expenses; the loss has been practically on interest only. During the last two or three years, owing to the war, there has been some loss also on account of operating expenses. The loss on the Grand Trunk Pacific has been, in round numbers, $7,000,000 during the last few years, and that was practically on interest.

What capital amount does that represent? Surely you can tell us that. It is absurd to think that we are undertaking an enterprise of this -kind and no one can tell us what obligations we are assuming. The Government -is afraid t-o say that we are assuming obligations for fear that it might interfere with our credit. I am not asking them to say that. But what capital amount are we assuming?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: On page 38 it is given exactly in several items.
What is the amount?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have told the hon. gentleman half a dozen times that you cannot lump these figures all together unless you want to deceive the House. Whether the hon. gentleman wants me to do that I do not know. Certain of these obligations we assume and agree to pay; the rest we do not. I have read both. I told the Committee what we agreed to pay and what the Grand Trunk Company had to, which

we had not assumed at all. The totals are: Capital stock, $60,833,332.51. The interest upon that at 4 per cent we guarantee to pay. Funded debt, $155,373,806.20. The interest on most of that is at 4 per cent and -some at 5 per cent, which we agree to pay.
What is the total?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am giving it to you now, but I will venture the prediction that the hon. -gentleman will want it at least six times more before we are sure. I have stated what we agree to pay.
Now, the property is- subject -to the list of obligations, that I read in detail and that amount to $18,184,738.42, of the nature of bonds, etc., on properties they acquired. Then it is subject to other obligations amounting to- $5,344,,207.54 in the nature of trust notes on equipment; other obligations in the nature of short-term loans amounting to- $35,548,235.08, -and other obligations in the nature of current liabilities. The property is not -subject to these last. They belong to- another distinct clasa again that we do not assume in any way but which the fixed -assets must be liable for before there is any equity. These current liabilities amount to $22,801,474.35. To say that we must pay interest on all of that is merely to talk humbug, because on the other side of the balance sheet are current assets enough to discharge these obligations. Surely the hon. ^gentleman understands a balance sheet. It has been before him. There are current -assets, in the nature of sundry outstanding accounts amounting to $43,838,831.44 which, as- the hon. gentleman knows, stand off *against the current liabilities. There are outstanding traffic accounts, amounting to $1,581,852.15 and materials and supplies cn hand, $6,407,195.57, all standing against current liabilities. Then there are "advances to controlled companies", and so on,-that appears on both sides -and these items are mot liabilities,-"Traders sidings bearing interest", and so on;-the assets and liabilities are there, they stand against each other. What is important is: What are the assets upon which we assume liability? What is funded against the property? I have given to the hon. gentleman the actual figures three or four times tonight.	.
What about the Grand Trunk Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have given him the Grand Trunk Pacific. We find a balance sheet showing exactly the same thing in

respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific, page 42. As 1 have explained what a balance sheet means in regard t<* the Grand Trunk I need not add that it means exactly the same thing in regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific.

The minister is not proposing that we shall assume interest payments on our own loans to the Grand Trunk Pacific? What is the amount of our loans to be deducted from the obligations of the Grand Trunk Pacific that we assume?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Our loans are all set
out on page 42 and the figures are just as plain as my words could be. The Grand Trunk Pacific is subject to all these liabilities. It has 'certain assets. In my opinion the assets are not at all equal to the liabilities but I am not responsible for that. So far did the liabilities exceed the assets on the Grand Trunk Pacific as a going concern that last year's deficit, including fixed charges, was over $10,000,000. There i& something in the nature of a monument. I would call it a monumental folly.

I presume the
Government intends to hold the Governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta liable for their guarantees of bonds ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
These governments are liable in relation to certain guarantees. The Dominion Government has not relieved them. I do not know that the matter of their liability is a serious one as far as the provinces are concerned, for the reason that the Government, although it does not assume the liability as an obligation of the Crown, it does, as a matter of practice take care of the road as a
going concern. Consequently, I think these provinces are justified in believing that their position is improved by the Government taking over the road.
Have they paid any interest ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. The Grand Trunk Pacific paid its own liabilities because the Government of Canada has lent it the money with which to pay. Consequently, the provinces have not been called upon to pay.
I understand the Grand Trunk Pacific defaulted some time ago. Have the provinces not been called upon since then?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend the
Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) informs me that since the Grand Trunk Pacific went into the hands of a receiver the two Governments have had to pay the maturing interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The governments ot
Saskatchewan and Alberta have had to take care of the interest.

I asked the Minister
yesterday how much the Grand Trunk had expended per mile of road for maintenance in comparison with the Canadian Pacific during the years 1915, 1916, 1917, 1918. Is he able to give me the information?
