By taking over the Grand Trunk, the Government assumes a capital obligation of about $400,000,000 and annual charges of $20,000,000. In acquiring the Grand Trunk Pacific its capital obligation would he increased' by about $300,000,000, and its expenses toy at least $8,000,000. This means that by such a proposed course of government ownership, the enormous debt of Canada would be increased by one third of its present amount. When we take these facts into consideration, in connection with the annual deficit of at least $20,000,000 in the case of the Canadian Northern, which has been acquired by the assumption of $434,312,747 of liabilities, including a bonded debt of $327,000,000, and the deficit in operating expenses of the Canadian Government railways, 'amounting in 1916 to $6,000,000 and over, without the payment of any interest on capital, it can easily be seen that the drain upon the Dominion treasury will soon -make heavy calls upon the taxpayers of -this country.
'The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) stated to Parliament on April 3, 1919, that if the Government should exercise its right of foreclosure on the Grand Trunk Pacific on the basis of its first -mortgage, and offer the road for sale, it could buy it at a much lower price than is represented by all the securities which have been issued in respect of it (Annual Report to Department of Railways -and Canals, 1917, p. 6). *H-e acknowledged then that if the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Railway on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific were fully taken into account, the value of the Grand Trunk shares, that is, the shareholders' equity in the -property, would be practically nil (Hansard, March 20, 1919, p. 701). The Government, therefore, has come to the

conclusion that the value of the assets in these cases is not a determining factor in the proposed change from private to public ownership. In other words, the Government encourages the -allegation -that it is a case for generosity, and not for exacting the full pound of flesh. I may add that the full pound of flesh will be exacted from, Canadians.
The ex-Minister of Finance also said that if the Government should take over the -Grand Trunk, and the same thing applies to the Grand Trunk Pacific, it would take it on the same basis as the Canadian Northern, that is, it would still be a corporation with power to issue securities when necessary. As -a corporation, its object would be to finance itself as much -as -possible. In this way, it seems, the Government is endeavouring to make the people think that they will not be obligated to the extent I -have shown, but that all the financial strain will rest upon the existing corporation, -which is in control of the properties. This confusing of the issue, is wholly derogatory to democratic government, which rests upon full and -accurate publicity. Does the Canadian Northern still do all its financing by the issuance of its securities and their sale in New York and London? I pause for an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It does part of its financing, selling equipment bonds, for instance, in Nerw York or any other -market it wishes.

Far from it, and the
Government knows it well. Then, why should this blind be held out, as a consequence of which many of the electorate are deceived? I have not argued either for or against public ownership, but have sought to -give the figures and the financial status of the railways in an unprejudiced manner, and the people of this country can draw their own conclusions.
It is regrettable that the Government has seen fit to bring down this railway legislation. Sir, we met here to approve of the Peace Treaty, and we have approved of it, even the Austrian Treaty which we have not seen and which was never presented to us. However ridiculous this session has been regarding the Peace Treaty, we wanted to finish with the war junkers, and work again once more in peace and harmony. To me this session appears like a hopeless joke. It was only planned to fool the people with another railway deal. Just as soon as a glimmer of light was beginning to penetrate the war -gloom, -and at the very time when the country needs wise discernment and

patriotic endeavour in its counsels, more so than at any other time since Confederation, the Government sees fit to force Parliament to grant them a blank cheque to crowd huge financial obligations on this country, on top of our enormous debt which now runs into the billions.
Sir, this is not the first time that the Government has outraged decency. It is not the first time that this beautiful Unionist aggregation, with its majority, has sacrificed Canada's interest to enrich speculators and rescue imprudent backers of that Bol-shivish financial clique of Toronto. It is not the first time that the Canadian people have been swayed by the sophistries of this unscrupulous Government.
It is not very long ago that we had to listen to stock arguments of all hon. gentlemen on your right, Sir, telling us about the glorious memories of Vimy, Cource-lette, Ypres, and Passchendaele, the bravery of Canadians on the battlefields and their gallant fights for freedom. "The last man; the last dollar"-this wa* the war-cry. The soldiers have come back, and no more a sound shall we hear from those sweet lutes. Ofittimes have we heard even the ex-Minister of Finance, whom we delight to hear, as we heard him this afternoon, mention the soldiers. But that nightingale also has been silenced'. He went up to the soldiers' committee and told them that there was no more money for the boys. But, Sir, there is money for the Toronto clique. This legislation may go through or not by means of the gag-machine; it matters not. We know very well that this Government will never put railway legislation through without applying the gag rule. But, Sir, when the next Budget is made public the people of Canada will realize in a shocking way that we are navigating troubled waters and that the currents on which we *are drifting sweep over more debts and deficits to the rocks of calamity and disaster. Hon. gentlemen opposite may have shaken hands to carry on the war to a successful end. That was a noble cause, but if they have formed a sort of family compact to drive Canada to the rocks of bankruptcy to enrich speculators, then, I say to those hon. gentlemen that individual greed should not govern this country any longer. I crave your pardon, Mr. Chairman, if I have trespassed unduly on the time of the committee, but I have endeavoured to express in my humble way my opinions on this subject.

With the indulgence of the members of the Cabinet, there are two or
three more questions which I shall ask, and then I hope I shall be through. The first point I should like to have elucidated is this: Taking the present net earnings of the Grand Trunk railway and the interest which we shall have to pay upon the debenture stock and guaranteed stock, which amounts to between $9,000,000 and $10,000,000, what is the deficit, subtracting the net income for the year 1917-18 from the interest which we shall have to pay upon the debenture stock and guaranteed stock? Is my question clear?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is clear, but why does the hon. gentleman pick out two of the worst years in the company's1 history? Would it not be fair to pick out ten?
I am taking only the last two years.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, because they were war years when no railway in the world made anything. Then, again, they were the years in which the McAdoo award took effect, and in this country the increase in rates did not take effect until much later. The hon. gentleman will hardly argue that it was fair to any invested capital, be it Canadian or foreign, to assume that it would stay in such an abnormal condition as that, or that any country would be justified in allowing it to do so. If the hon. gentleman takes, as the Drayton-Acworth report asks should be done, ten years, and even includes in them certain war years, then there will be more than sufficient to pay all obligations, all debts, interest on guaranteed stock, and more besides.

Can the minister inform me why the Grand Trunk Railway has altogether suspended the payment of dividends on the guaranteed stock and debenture stock for the last two years, as appears in this booklet?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They did not. They
paid interest on debenture stock. Guaranteed interest was not paid in 1917-18 for the reasons I have given, because there was no money to pay it with. There was a small surplus but they did not declare dividends for very clear reasons which I have given. The hon. gentleman should not assume that any company was a failure merely because it had paid no interest on certain portions of its capital stock last year and the year before. If so there would be scarcely a sound railway in the world; there would not be one in the United States or in England, as I am informed. There would be in Canada, on account of the tremendous land assets and the very strong position of the Canadian

Pacific railway, a position very largely due to the extraordinary generous treatment received at the hands of this Dominion.

I do not want the inference to be drawn that the company would be insolvent for that reason. I suppose the failure to pay interest must be attributed to the decrease in the earnings and the increase in the runing expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. I think the hon.
gentleman will find that the earnings were the greatest then that they ever had and that the amount of traffic was the highest. The amount of service rendered this country was the greatest that the Grand Trunk ever rendered. But owing chiefly to the McAdoo award as to the wages* applying in Canada by virtue of our law, and to the increased cost of operation generally, due to increased cost of supply, the entire earnings of the company were eaten into except to the extent of a small surplus.
Is the minister taking any stock in the Drayton-Acworth report, which says that in 1917 the sum of_ $21,000,000. was necessary to put the road in good condition and for improvements generally?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. The Drayton-
Acworth report would not say that because it was published in 1916.
Well, whenever it was published.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member wants to know if I am taking any stock in the report in that respect?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Our contention will be that the report is right. The Grand Trunk, however, strenuously contend that it is wrong, and brings considerable evidence forward to that effect. They certainly have not convinced Sir Henry Drayton, who was largely responsible for the report. As to where the exact line lies, I am not competent to say. The arbitration board will have to determine that.

The Minister of the Interior said a moment ago that we did not in any way assume the liabilities of the company. This is absolutely right. But, on the other hand, I think his statement calls for explanation. I shall express my view of the situation and should like to be corrected if I am wrong. Technically speaking the Dominion of Canada is not by any means assuming the liabilities of the company, but it is making an investment to the amount of $216,000,000 by becoming responsible in

perpetuity for the payment of the interest on the debenture stock and the guaranteed stock, which together represent a capitalization of $216,000,000. Now, in the agreement we say that we are going to pay forever the interest on this sum.
For the sake of argument we may say that we are making an investment of $216,000,000. Besides that we shall be making an investment to the extent of the amount of the award of the arbitrators. If the award is for $10,000,000 we shall invest that sum because we shall give stock for it. By making ourselves responsible in perpetuity for the payment of the interest on the debenture stock and the guaranteed stock we are making an investment of $216,000,000. If the award is $10,000,000 our investment in the Grand Trunk railway will be $226,000,000 and it is so much of an investment that, suppose through some calamity the Grand Trunk railway system should disappear from the face of the earth, we would be' losing $226,000,000. If the physical property should disappear we would owe the shareholders the interest forever just the same as we owe the interest on the mortgage on a house after the house has been burned. There is no getting out of it that we are making an investment of over $200,000,000.
Of course, there are on the other side, assets which we must take account of as the hon. the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) said this afternoon. We are not assuming the other liabilities of the company, but by becoming the most interested party in this concern, we are practically assuming the other liabilities because we could not afford to let the road go into liquidation or insolvency. Let us suppose that the $22,000,000 current liabilities, as they appear at page 39 of the booklet, should not be paid, and that the holders of these securities should ask the qompany to be put into liquidation and into the hands of a receiver; the Government could not afford to let the company go into the hands of a receiver because, if it should be sold far below its value, the Government would be in danger of losing the $226,000,000 which it has invested. Consequently, we are in the same position as the man who would take a second mortgage of $5,000 on a $10,000 house. He might very well say, " I am not interested in the first mortgage; I have nothing to do with it." That is true. He is not assuming any responibility as to the first mortgage, but in reality he is responsible for the first mortgage if he wants to save his own second mortgage. We are not assuming the other liabilities of the

company but because our interest goes with these liabilities, because we have to secure the interests of the company and because we have to save the company, we make ourselves responsible practically for the whole of the liabilities of the company. That is my point of view and if I am mistaken I should like to be corrected.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The speech of the hon. gentleman convinces me that he very clearly understands the situation. I do not say that he expresses it quite correctly, but I believe that in his own head it is just as clear as it can be in the mind of any hon. member. While it is not quite correct to say as he says that we are making an investment of $216,000,000 because we are agreeing to pay the interest on that amount already invested, still the very statement of that shows that he understands just what we are doing. We are agreeing to pay interest on that money which is already invested. That differs from investing it in this very important feature that we do not have to find the money and we could not find it to-day without an expenditure of considerably more than that amount. It is much more advantageous to us than if we had to find $216,000,000 and invest it. If we had to find and invest it on a four per cent basis, it would cost us more than $216,000,000. It might cost us about $250,000,000. While the hon. member evinces a clear understanding of the situation he does not put it in a correct way, but I knoiv that he understands clearly that as I am stating it to him now I am putting it in the correct way. As to what he says about other obligations-obligations standing against the properties of the Grand Trunk Railway Company which we are taking over-his conception in that regard is quite correct. They do not become an obligation of the Government, but the Grand Trunk would have to take care bf them in order to protect its own interests, and the Government is the stockholder of the Grand Trunk. What the hon. member has in mind* is quite right. That is the position of the Grand Trunk has been in all these years. It is the position that every road in the world is in. There is not a road in the worljl that owns its properties subject to nothing. Against properties taken over there are perpetual obligations. We are going to be in that position when we take over the Grand Trunk. It is a pleasure to answer any question put by my hon. friend because there is some result in the answer.

From the discussion last night I got the impression, which perhaps was an entirely wrong one, that the market price of the stocks of the Grand Trunk might play some part in fixing the value which the Government would be called upon to acknowledge by way of hew guaranteed stock. Reading over the report in Hansard, I am not certain that the inference is correctly drawn, but I believe that certain other hon. gentlemen in the House are under the same impression, and I thought it would be well to have it set right by a direct statement from the minister. To my mind the market prices of these stocks to-day, or six months, or a year from to-day, can have nothing whatever to do with the value of the property. I presume-I may be quite wrong-that the board of arbitration will inquire into the physical assets of this corporation, its right of way, terminal facilities, equipment and so forth, will set up against these various obligations that may exist in one form or another, and will strike a balance on this basis: After these obligations are met what is the equity to be assigned to the various preference and common stocks? It is well known that for .years Grand Trunk stock on the London market has been a speculative counter. The market has been rigged more than once more or less on current newspaper information, and it would be easy, particularly when there is such a large number of shareholders, to cause a violent fluctuation in any one class of these stocks. So that, to my mind, it would be entirely misleading should the idea go abroad that the market price of the stocks "has anything to do with their value.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The view expressed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cronyn) is almost identically my own. The market value, in my judgment, if it is to be considered a factor at all-that is a subject for evidence -would be a very minor matter before the arbitration tribunal. It is quite true, as the hon. gentleman says, that market value on the stock exchange is a very poor guide as to what the real value is, because the quotations are influenced by speculative considerations so very largely that it would seem to me it would be next to valueless evidence as to what the stocks were really worth. While that is my opinion, the answer would not be complete unless I added that according to the resolution and according to the letters both of July 18th and October 10th, the arbitration tribunal necessarily must be itself the judge as to



what evidence is and as to what weight is to be attached to evidence when admitted. That is to say the arbitration tribunal is the judge as to what kind of evidence can be admitted to prove value. It would have power to wholly strike out all evidence as to market value, and if it decides that the evidence can be admitted it is the sole judge as to what weight can be given to it. So, while in my opinion, the arbitration tribunal should give very little, if any, weight at all to it, and perhaps should not admit it, that is altogether for it to say- the matter is in its hands, and rightly so.
Will there be an appeal from the award of the arbitrators?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There will be if the award is not unanimous, but only on a question of law. If the other side claims that the arbitrators adopted a wrong legal principle in coming to their conclusion, then they have an appeal to the Supreme Court in the event of the award not being unanimous.
If the arbitrators are unanimous there is no appeal either on a question of law or on a question of fact?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I must confess to a feeling of surprise at the principle my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) has laid down with reference to the ownership of property. I have always been under the impression that I owned a house, but I have never held it free from mortgage since I bought it. Notwithstanding that I have never had any doubt about my ownership, nor has anybody else so far as I am aware.

Does not my hon.
friend know, as a lawyer, that the legal estate in that house is absolutely in the mortgagee?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I know that, technically, the legal estate goes to the mortgagee.
Absolutely.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
But that does not Change the fact as to who is the real owner of the property. The, mortgagee has only his claim upon the house, which may be paid when it becomes due. Therefore all that my hon. friend has said amounts to this, that we are buying a property which according to this statement represents an investment in road and equipment of $434,990,999; that there are certain charges and obligations upon that property; and that in acquiring the stock of the company we get the benefit of the equity, that is, the difference between the value of the assets and of the liabilities. That is perfectly true, and no one has said anything to the contrary. There is not a railway on this continent, I do not think there is a railway in Great Britain, that is not in exactly the same situation. I do not know of any railway that has not bond issues outstanding. The Canadian Pacific Railway has such issues. It is the regular method of financing a road. The result is that there are of course these obligations outstanding against the road; but, as my hon. friends, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) pointed out so clearly yesterday, in valuing the stock the arbitrators must take into consideration the obligations of the company as well as its assets, because the stock has no value until all obligations are discharged.
If the company were liquidated, all these claims must be paid before the stockholders would receive a dollar. Therefore, in estimating the value of the stock, the arbitrators must take into consideration all the outstanding obligations, and they would find a value in the stock only if they reached the conclusion that, after considering the value of the assets, putting opposite

them the value of the liabilities, there was still an equity in the road which would be represented by the stock in the road, and they would fix the value of that equity. That seems to be a perfectly clear position as has already been outlined by my colleagues. That is the situation in this case. The arbitrators are to determine, after considering the assets and the liabilities, what value attaches to those stocks which give us control of the road, and they must consider every one of the items which are set out in this schedule. My hon. friend has referred to one particular item, and he has questioned whether that asset is worth a hundred cents on the dollar. I do not know the details of that item, but what I say to my hon. friend is that the arbitrators must go into that; they must look into those assets and those liabilities, and evidence will be submitted by the Government with reference to this. The agreement will provide that the Government shall have full access to all the books of the company, and to all its accounts, in order that the Government may prepare its case. In addition, during the period that intervenes between the execution of the agreement and the making of the award, the management of the company will be in the hands of a committee of management, two of the members of which will be appointed by the Government and two by the Grand Trunk, these four to appoint a fifth. Therefore, the Government will have the fullest opportunity to investigate the value of all these assets, every item in the schedule, to investigate all the liabilities, to check them up, to ascertain if they have been fully disclosed and to lay all this information before the arbitrators in order that they may find the value of the stock. Then a further provision has been inserted in the letter, and will be embodied in the agreement to protect the Government against any possible liability cropping up after the award is made. While the Government will have an opportunity of some months to investigate all the books, to check up every liability, to see that everything is fully disclosed, yet, even after the award is made, if they find within three months, when they are in full possession of the road, any liability which has not been disclosed-the matter is referred back to the Board of Arbitrators, which is kept- in existence for that period- for reconsideration, and it will be their duty to modify their award in so far as they feel that this liability calls for a modification. Therefore, the Government has protected

the situation on every point to meet the case which my hon. friend has suggested.
Just one word with reference to the evidence which would go before the arbitrators. My hon. friend has said that he thinks the arbitrators would be bound, I judge from his observations, to determine value on the market value.

I said that would be
evidence.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it is open to argument that it is evidence that can be submitted to the arbitrators. Personally I do not question that. I think it is open to the arbitrators, as the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) has said, to receive any evidence which they believe will enable them to ascertain value. But I point out to my hon. friend, in addition to the considerations presented by the Minister of the Interior, why that evidence would be unreliable, why that evidence would not be good evidence on. which to base an award. The price at which you can sell 100 shares or 200 shares or 500 shares of stock on a market is absolutely no criterion as to the price at which you can sell 5100,000,000 in shares. You * may have a market that will absorb a few shares; but if you commence to put tens of thousands of shares on the * market, you completely demoralize it, and the price sinks down, as any one who knows anything of the conditions of a stock market will realize.

My hon. friend knows
that you can glut any market of anything.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If you are selling a few shares of stock, say 100 shares, then I will concede to my hon. friend that the selling price on the stock market might toe a very important consideration; but when you are selling shares involving nearly 5200,000,000, you have a wholly different proposition. The price at which 10, or 100, or 1,000 shares might be sold on the market is no criterion of the market price of this larger block in case you put it on the market. What I would submit to my hon. friend is that the real evidence as to the value of the shares will depend upon two considerations; first, th$ value of the assets as against the liabilities, and second, the earnings of the company. Because it is only out of the earnings, present or prospective, that dividends can be paid. Therefore, the question of earnings would be the most important consideration which the arbitrators would be called upon to take into account in determining
the value of the stock, plus the value of the assets and the liabilities. As my hon. friend has mentioned, the arbitrators would be the judges of the evidence to be admitted to enable them to arrive at a determination of value.
Just one or two other observations and I am through, not in answer to my hon. friend, but in answer to an observation of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding).
I understand the President of the Council stood up to answer my question. His speech is very nice, but I should like an answer.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I understood my hon. friend had finished.
I had finished, but I had finished by asking a question.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was going to answer^ an observation of the hon. member for/ Shelburne and Queen's.
And come back to my question?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thought I had answered my hon. friend's question.

My hon. friend must have forgotten what I said, or I must have been very stupid. What I asked my hon. friend was: How much money have we to pay to get a clear title to the physical assets of the road that we are going to buy?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If the Government wanted to clear off the obligations existing, so as to have a road wholly free from any obligations, and that no railway in this country possesses

	,
The Intercolonial is absolutely free. Put this road in the position of the Intercolonial.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will find the obligations set out on pages 38 and 39.
I am not paid for adding up those obligations, as the minister is.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am under the impression that my hon. friend is better paid than the minister. I think if my hon. friend will undertake that addition, the compensation will be equal to the work, and he will find all the obligations set out on those pages.
That is the best answer the minister will give?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot give any more. The liabilities are ail set out on those pages.

Any ordinary man looking over these figures cannot be sure he has .got them right, because things are so mixed up that there is danger of making a mistake, but if we can get the information from a member of the Government we can assume that it is right.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My bon. friend is just as capable as I am of reading English, and perhaps some other language in addition. Take the 4 per cent guaranteed stock, for instance. There is no necessity for our ever redeeming that. All we have to do is to pay the 4 per cent on it, but if we desired to redeem it we would have to pay such a price as the holders would be prepared to accept. We are entitled to redeem this stock at par at any time after a period of thirty years.

That is- not what I was speaking of. Take the first item on page 39, for instance, second mortgage equipment bonds. That is against the equipment, I suppose. What would it amount to if we had to pay off that?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will see that the first item of $241,257,000 we do not have to pay. We will have to pay, of course, 4 per cent on whatever amount the arbitrators fix for the first, second and third preference and the common stocks. That is all we will have to pay on these items. The funded debt of $155,000,000 is a permanent obligation. If we wished to retire it, and the parties were prepared to accept par for it, we would have to pay $155,000,000. It may be they would be prepared to take less than par; I cannot say. It is a funded obligation perpetual in its character, bearing a certain rate of interest. Nobody could say what we could get it for at the present time, but there is a provision in the agreement whereby we can retire it at par at the end of thirty years, or any time thereafter if we wish to do so. Then the next item, second mortgage equipment bonds, Northern third mortgage, Canada Atlantic bonds, and so on, amounting to $18,000,000 odd-we could redeem those in accordance with the terms of the securities. The next is an advance by the Canadian Government. That is an obligation of the company to us. The other obligations we coulu retire in accordance with the terms set out on the face of the securities. I cannot add them together without taking into consideration the character of each. You cannot give a total in that sense, because the nature of the obligation is different, as the Minister of the Interior so clearly pointed out this afternoon; but all the information is contained there.
IMr. Rowell.]
Coming now to the observation of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) he said Ije believed the people of this country were against the Government going on with this proposal. I notice in to-day's issue of the Toronto Globe a short editorial entitled " Liberalism and Public Ownership," and my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) and possibly some other members on the other side may be interested in hearing what the Globe says.
It has no effect on me.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The editorial says:
The general feeling of opposition to public ownership in Quebec, which is, largely responsible for the opposition of the Liberal party to the acquisition of the Grand Trunk, is utterly at variance with the feeling of Liberals in Ontario and the western provinces. The people of Ontario, irrespective of party lines, are strongly in favour of the coupling up of the Grand Trunk with the Canadian National system.
I believe that fairly represents the opinion of the people of Ontario and Western Canada.
That is the opinion of one man sitting behind a curtain at a little desk in the Globe office. We do not know who he is at all.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Quite so, but as the
paper supports my hon. friends on the other side of the House it is an indication of the feeling in Ontario. This is the feeling in Ontario and Western Canada-I do not profess to speak for the feeling of the province of Quebec
The Globe does not always speak for Ontario, I am sorry to say.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, sometimes it is right, and sometimes it is wrong. In this case I believe it is right.

What about the Montreal
Star?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The editorial proceeds:
The country hae on its hands a great mileage of unprofitable railways on the borders of settlement which may not in our time earn interest upon the capital Invested. The only hope of preventing a continuous drain of the national revenue for the payment of railway deficits is by the incorporation in the National railway system of a road such as the Grand Trunk, which taps the rich traffic-producing areas of Quebec and Ontario, and has an established long haul traffic between the seaboard and the interior of the United States and Canada.
I believe that statement fairly represents the feeling of the great majority of the people of Ontario and Western Canada, ir-

respective of party. Liberals and Conservatives alike recognize the national necessity of acquiring this road, and are prepared to support the policy of the Government in acquiring it. There are only three possible alternatives. First, the liquidation of the road. The Grand Trunk could go into a receiver's hands as the Grand Trunk Pacific has, that is a possibility, because the Grand Trunk has admitted it cannot continue to discharge its obligations in respect of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I do not believe the people of Canada are prepared for that or desire to see it brought about. Second, there is the possibility of the road going into the hands of the Canadian Pacific. I do not believe the people of Canada are prepared to have their whole railway system in the hands of one corporation, no matter how efficient that corporation may be.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The people of Canada
are not prepared to have the whole transportation system of this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific in the hands of any one corporation and be subjected to the control that that corporation might exercise over the people by controlling all our transportation system. The third course is government ownership, the taking over of this road by the Government. Those are the only three courses open, and the last one is the one in the national interest and I believe has the support of an overwhelming majority of the people of this country.

I asked, with the very best intentions and with a sincere desire for information to be enlightened, as to how much we have to pay in order to put this new road, if we are going to acquire it, in the same position as the Intercolonial. I mention the Intercolonial because there is no difficulty in understanding the situation there. The road is owned by the Government and there is no claim of any kind against it. My hon. friend (Mr. Rowell) made a very clever speech, as he always can make, but, as we say in common parlance in Nova Scotia, kept away from the pig as far as he could. On page 39, if I can trust my knowledge of figures, I find _ that we have to pay $504,629,211.93. We have to pay that anyhow before we have the road clear.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, my hon. friend will
see that included in that figure is all the preference and common stock. There is $116,000,000 of the common stock alone, and the first, second and third preference,
amount in all to about $63,000,000 or $64,000,000. So that you commence with $184, 000,000 taken off. We do not have to pay that. All we will have to pay is whatever the arbitrators may fix as the value of that $184,000,000 or $185,000,000 of. stock. You take that off to start with.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And then take off the current liabilities and the advances to controlled companies. All these things are balanced on the other side. They are just cross entries. Even in the case of the Intercolonial there are current liabilities, but there are current assets against them. The same is true here. There are current liabilities of some $22,000,000, and on the other side current assets of some $51,000,000. So that we do not have to pay out of the Treasury of Canada that $22,000,000. If we wanted to clear the road off, which we could not likely do as the bonds are perpetual, we would have to pay the $35,000,000 odd, the $5,000,000, the $173,000,000 and the $60,000,000.
What is this item of $43,000,000? Would that include the claim of the Grand Trunk against the Grand Trunk Pacific on account of advances?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Scarcely, because it is an asset.
I am referring to the claim of the Grand Trunk against the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know what
the details of that $43,000,000 are but I presume it would include any claim provided it was not a set-off. It will also include cash on hand and amounts owing for other than traffic. In a word, the company's gross earnings in a year would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $60,000,000. At any single time there are tremendous current assets. A detailed statement could be given of the $43,838,000 current assets, showing just what they are. Perhaps it is in the book, but if it is not the statement can be secured.

That is very important. It is quite an item, and if that $43,000,000 is merely an offset against the Grand Trunk Pacific it would not he considered as an asset in connection with the assets of the Grand Trunk, because there would be no possibility of collecting it. Another item is outstanding traffic accounts, $1,500,000. That would be freight receipts not in yet; but the $43,000,000 could not be current traffic items. It is a large amount. If it

means Grand Trunk Pacific obligations it is of very little value in this transaction, and when you talk about liabilities you must take into account the Grand Trunk Pacific liabilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The information that
the hon. gentleman asks for I will have for him to-morrow, but I hardly think it would be fair to take the last season's operations in connection with the Intercolonial, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern and use them as arguments as indicating the position of any of these railways in normal times. During last year all of the railways were subjected to very high operating costs owing to the McAdoo award. The increased cost of labour was very high. It was not only the labour; it was fuel and every item- that one could mention in connection with the operation of railways, and the cost was very much higher than in normal times.
And the freight rates were not increased. In fact, if I remember rightly, part of the time, I think it was last year, as a result of the McAdoo award and other causes, the cost of operating the roads was increased, whereas the freight rates were not increased at all. It would hardly be fair to take the cost of the operation of those roads f-or the past year and on that basis judge what is likely to happen in the case of the Grand Trunk, the Canadian- Northern, and the Grand Trunk Pacific in the future. So far -as the Intercolonial is concerned, prior to the war it was doing very well. The same condition was true of the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern, but for reasons I have stated conditions last year were abnormal and it should not be taken as a fair year in discussing this matter.
With reference to the Grand Trunk railway I want to emphasize this point: I have taken the matter up with the president of that company personally and have had him

state in writing the condition of the Grand Trunk Railway system. That letter is as follows:
Montreal, October 16, 1919.
Replying to your Inquiry of this morning: the Grand Trunk Railway system, including both Canadian and American lines, is in excellent physical condition, in respect to track, bridges, and buildings, and will, in the immediate future, require only normal expenditures for its maintenance. The same remarks apply to the condition of its motive power and equipment. The condition of the Grand Trunk Railway system in these respects will compare favourably with that of any railroad, either in Canada or the United States, having the same character and density of traffic.
Yours faithfully,
OSgd.) Howard G. Kelly.
Did my hon. friend expect him to say anything else when he was selling the road?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This statement is in writing over his own signature, and he will have to prove it before the arbitrators. In addition to that, I may say that our own Canadian National railway experts have been travelling over the Grand Trunk and they report in verbal conversations to me that the system is really in good condition and would compare with any of our own systems. It must be remembered that the Intercolonial ran down during the last four or five years for the reason that we could not get rails or ties. Neither could we get the men necessary to keep the road in the condition in which it was prior to the war.
So much the worse for government ownership.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
However, we kept the Intercolonial in as good a state as the other roads, which could not get rails either.
With reference to the information that the hon. gentleman has asked for, I can get it for him in a very short time in the morning, and I therefore wish to ask
11 p.m. if he entertains any objection to the committee reporting the resolution so that the Bill may be introduced forthwith. The measure has to go through its first and second readings and then be considered in committee when the matter, of course, can come up for discussion again, but by the acceptance of my suggestion the proceedings can-be advanced. That will not interfere with the getting of any information which has been requested; there is no desire at all to hurry the Bill; I merely make the suggestion with a view of advancing the proceedings.

I may say to the minister that I usually have a great deal of

trouble in getting any information after I have allowed him to cross the bridge.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Not intentionally, I
hope.

I allowed the Bill to go through the other day with the promise of the leader of the Government that I would get certain information from the Minister of Railways. I got some of that information, but only about five per cent of wnat I was looking for. Now I am afraid, if I put myself in the same position again and allow the resolution to pass there will not be very much rush in the minister's office to get the information sought.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Bill will have to be considered in committee and we shall be exactly in the same position, as regards discussion, that we now are, because the measure contains the same clauses that are in the resolution. I think I can assure the hon. gentleman that I will send a messenger down by twelve o'clock to-morrow with the information he has asked for this evening. Moreover, I will not ask that the Bill be reported from committee until the hon. gentleman is perfectly satisfied that all the information he has asked for, or that he may want at that time, is given to him.

I want to have a distinct understanding from the minister as to when we may expect the information for which I am asking, and I would like to add to what I have already stated that I think it would be well to put in concise form the real obligations of the road under consideration, apart from the stock altogether, that is, the obligations that appear on pages 38 and 39, and also on pages 51 and 52 of the blue-book which was put into the hands of hon. members yesterday. What is the real amount in dollars and cents of the obligations we are assuming in connection with the other liabilities against the road, should this transaction go through? The minister will remember and will find in Hansard the otheT question that I asked. The minister said that it was not a fair comparison; that those were not favourable years. I am sure that he is submitting his evidence, at all events as far as the hon. gentlemen sitting on your right are concerned, to a favourable and sympathetic jury, and I am sure they will take fully into consideration every element in the facts that can be construed favourably to the minister. Whether the facts are agreeable or disagreeable, whether we are making money or losing money, nothing should be concealed from the House or from the people in regard to the business of the people, particularly as concerns those roads. If the case is bad, we ought to know it; if a patient is sick unto death, it will be well for him to prepare for his eternal rest and know exactly his position. If this country is on the verge of a smash by reason of bad financing, we might as well know it and prepare for the worst. I think it is only fair Ao let us know just exactly how we stand in connection with the information for which I am asking. If the minister will undertake that at the opening of the House to-morrow we shall have that information, I have not the slightest inclination to interfere with the progress of this Bill. Knowing all the time that I am against

it and purpose voting against it at every stand, I do not wish to take up time beyond what is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The hon. member is very clear in what he has just suggested, and I can assure him that I will get all the information and hand it to him before the House meets to-morrow; otherwise I will not ask him to proceed with the matter any further. He is absolutely right that the House is entitled to all information in connection with the operation of the roads that he has mentioned, or any other roads.
The information has all been made public, and it is simply a question of getting it from the records. It would take only a few moments' time. I would ask the hon. member if he has any objection to this: He will remember that I gave notice to-day of an . amendment to this resolution, as follows:
That the following proposed amendment he referred to the Committee of the Whole on the proposed resolutions in respect to the acquisition by His Majesty of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada:-
''12. That the Government may make, out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund, any expenditure necessary in the preparation for, and conduct of, the arbitration proceeding herein provided for."
In the resolution as it stands we omitted to make monetary provision for the arbitration proceedings as we went along, and I therefore gave notice of the amendment I have just read. I am advised by the Deputy Speaker that in order to have this amendment embodied in the resolution now before us it will be necessary to move that the Committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again this day, when I will move:
That the order of the House that the House do go into Committee of the Whole to-morrow to consider a certain proposed amendment to the resolutions in respect to the acquisition by His Majesty of the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada be rescinded.
If my hon. friend has no objection, I now move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again this day.

One very serious objection I have to the proposed amendment is that it provides for moneys being utilized by the Government without having first been voted by Parliament. Now we have always fought against that. We. have said that every dollar expended by the Government should appear in the Estimates and receive the sanction of Parliament. The minister will remember that a 
year or so ago he was obliged to withdraw a resolution of this kind and abandon the idea of getting money out of the consolidated revenue fund without it being specifically voted for the purpose for which it was to be expended. That, I think, is the right principle, that no moneys shall be expended except upon a vote of Parliament. The principle of the proposed amendment is that we should give a free hand to the minister to take money out of the consolidated revenue fund without any specific vote, and I am opposed to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Under the circumstances I shall not press the matter further, but will found the Bill on the resolution now before the committee.
Resolution to report progress withdrawn.
Resolution for acquisition of the Grand Trunk Railway system agreed to, on division, reported, read the first and second time on division, and concurred in.
Mr. J. D. REID thereupon move! lor leave to introduce Bill No. 33, respecting the acquisition by His Majesty of the Grand Trunk Railway system.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 11.35 p. m.
Friday, October 17, 1919.
